name: Bandoline

lead: Bandoline is an old-fashioned hair-setting product with a gel-like, sticky consistency, used to hold hair, curls and mustaches in place. It predates modern hair gels and was a forerunner of later fixatives.
It helps looks by keeping a style smooth and set through the day. The hold lasts until washed out.

paras: Historically it was brushed or combed through hair and left to dry to set the style. Modern users interested in the vintage look generally use today's pomades and gels, which fill the same role.
Little modern information exists on the product itself. Styling products in general can cause scalp irritation or build-up in some people.

angle.text: Bandoline was used to hold hair in a smooth or curled shape. It gave a set, glossy finish that lasted through the day.

lead: Bandoline is a historical gel-like hair styling product, a setting liquid used to keep hair flat or curled in place. It sits in the lineage of hair fixatives that runs from fat-based ancient dressings to pomades and modern gels [1][2].

Hair styling gels have a long history: analysis of mummified hair found a fat-based gel in ancient Egypt, and a bog body from the Iron Age used a pine resin gel. In 1914 José Antonio Brancato in Buenos Aires made a gum-based fixative that gave the word gomina, and Brylcreem followed in 1929 [2].
Pomade popularity peaked between the 1920s and 1950s, and the Wikipedia pomade article lists bandoline as a related topic [1]. Little published material describes bandoline directly.

paras: Hair fixatives range from ancient fat-based gels [2] to eighteenth- and nineteenth-century pomades made mainly from bear fat or lard [1], to the water-based gels of the 1960s [2].

timeline.event: Gum-based fixative registered in Buenos Aires as gomina [2].
